title: Chand Kazi
html:
The Ruler of Navadvipa

When Sri Chaitanya roused Navadvipa to the kirtana of the holy name, the town was ruled by a Muslim whom the original sources call simply the Kazi. Krishnadasa Kaviraja also calls him by name, Chand Kazi (chanda kaji); Vrindavana Dasa says only "the Kazi"; the “Bhakti-ratnakara” calls him "a yavana named the Kazi", and Govinda-deva in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” "the yavana ruler" and "a mleccha". The biographies know him as Chand Kazi, and one of them, mindful of the mercy he received, heads its account of him "Bhakta Chand Kazi", "Chand Kazi the devotee". His personal name is given by Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati in the “Anubhashya” in two ways: by some accounts he was called Maulana Sirajuddin, by others Habibur Rahman.1

In Navadvipa the Kazi was both judge and ruler. The “Charitamrita” calls him the magistrate; in their conversation the Lord will say to him, "You are the Kazi; you have authority to oppose the Hindu religion," and the enemies of the kirtana, "You are the lord of the whole town; all its people are yours." Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that the Kazi was the faujdar, the head of the district. In those days the zamindars collected the revenue, while justice and government were in the hands of the kazis, and both were under the subadar of Bengal; the parganas of Nadia, Islampur and Bagoyan belonged to Hari Hor or to his descendant Krishnadasa Hor, but the Kazi had taken their government into his own hands. The biographies speak of him as the local ruler who held power in his hands, and one of them also as the local magistrate. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” relates that the yavana Kazi was very powerful, that Navadvipa and the country around were under his sway, that the people of that land trembled before him, and that no one could freely worship God (2.297–299).

He was close to the ruler of all Gauda as well. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says that the yavana king of Gauda loved him dearly and no one dared disobey the Kazi (2.298). This king, according to the “Anubhashya”, was Ala-ud-din Saiyad Husain Shah, at that time the independent ruler of Bengal (the “Anubhashya” gives the years of his reign as 1498–1511); the same commentary says that Chand Kazi is said to have been the teacher (guru) of the Nawab Husain Shah. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” and one of the biographies call the Padshah the Kazi's kinsman. And the Lord Himself, threatening the Kazi, will say: let Me see what his king will do (CB, Madhya 23.122, 400).

The Kazi's house stood in the village of Simulia, on the edge of Nadia: there, according to the “Chaitanya-bhagavata”, the night procession came before turning towards his house (Madhya 23.348, 359, 379). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” that Simulia lies a mile or so (one and a half kilometres) from the northern boundary of Ganganagara, and that in Simulia there still remains the lane of Vamana-pukura, where the Kazi's house stood, a house preserved to this day. Srila Bhaktivinoda speaks of the old house of the Kazi's family in the village of Brahmana-pushkarini, whose other part adjoins Taranavasa, formerly called Bilva-pushkarini. Jayananda too (in a retelling) remembers "the village of Simulia", where the Kazi's house was broken and from which the yavanas fled.

Nothing more is known of his life in the world. Neither the original sources nor the biographies name his parents or the place and year of his birth, nor do they say when he left this world. He has no days in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math. He appears in the narrative only in these days: when he forbade the kirtana, and on the night of the great procession to his house. The “Charitamrita” places these pastimes in the years between the Lord's sixteenth year and His sannyasa; Srila Bhaktivinoda calls this night "the night of the first town kirtana"; and by our timeline these are the years 1509–1510, when the Lord was twenty-three or twenty-four.

Kirtana in Every House

After His return from Gaya the Lord opened the holy name to all the townspeople. Vrindavana Dasa gives His words:

“‘Hare Krishna Hare Krishna Krishna Krishna Hare Hare / Hare Rama Hare Rama Rama Rama Hare Hare.’ The Lord went on: ‘This is the maha-mantra. Chant it, all of you, a fixed number of times. <…> Five or ten of you may gather in a house and hold kirtana, clapping your hands.’” (CB, Madhya 23.76–77, 79)

Srila Bhaktivinoda adds that the Lord first told those living near Srivasa to chant the name, clapping their hands; then mridangas and karatalas began to sound, and from that time the sankirtana spread from door to door. The “Charitamrita” says:

“When the Lord gave His order to the townspeople, they began to hold sankirtana in every house: ‘Hari haraye namah, krishna yadavaya namah, gopala govinda rama sri-madhusudana.’ The great sound of sankirtana rose with mridangas and karatalas, and nothing could be heard but ‘Hari! Hari!’” (CC, Adi 17.121–123)

The Lord, who seeks no honour for Himself and honours everyone (amani manada), embraced each one and asked them to sing the names. In the homes of pious families there were mridangas and conches: before, they had been played only in autumn or in the month of Chaitra, at pujas to Mahamaya performed for passing worldly gains. Now the same instruments served the unceasing Hari-kirtana, and worldly people, hearing them, took the singers for musicians "doing puja to Mahamaya out of season" and mocked them. So everything that had served worldly ends found its meaning in the service of the Lord.

The Broken Mridanga

One day the Kazi was passing along a road where the name was being sung. Vrindavana Dasa relates:

“One day, by the will of Providence, the Kazi was going along that road and heard the sound of mridangas, karatalas and conches. When the Kazi heard the loud sound of the holy name on every side, he at once remembered his own scriptures. The Kazi said, ‘Seize them, seize them! Today I shall do my work. Let us see what your Nimai Acharya will do today.’ The townspeople fled in confusion. <…> Whomever the Kazi caught, he beat. He broke the mridanga and made an outrage at the door.” (CB, Madhya 23.101–105)2

The “Charitamrita” tells it otherwise: the Muslims complained to the Kazi about the kirtana, and he came to one of the houses.

“In the evening the Kazi came angrily to one house, broke the mridanga and said to the people: ‘All this time no one here has dared to follow Hindu ways openly. Now you carry on with such zeal — on whose strength, I would like to know? Let no one hold kirtana anywhere in the town. Today I forgive you and go home. But if I find anyone holding kirtana again, I will take all he owns and strip him of his caste.’” (CC, Adi 17.125–128)3

Srila Bhaktivinoda explains these words: from the coming of Bakhtiyar Khilji until Chand Kazi, Hindu ways had been held down in Navadvipa, and believers would say "Hari" only in secret and fall silent. In Vrindavana Dasa the Kazi threatens: "Nadia has turned Hindu; when I catch them, I shall punish them. Today I forgive you, since night has fallen; another day I shall take away your caste" (CB, Madhya 23.106–107), and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that he was threatening to convert the townspeople to his faith by force.4 The ban delighted all the unbelievers, and they went on jeering at the devotees.

From then on the Kazi went about the town with his men every day, looking for kirtana — according to the “Chaitanya-bhagavata”, "with thousands of his followers" (Madhya 23.108, 116) — and the townspeople hid from him. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that he was helped in his search by sinful townspeople who envied the devotees. On his side too stood the unbelievers (pashandis), whom the acharya calls "so-called Hindus".5 They said, "The name of Hari should be repeated in the mind," and rejoiced that the Kazi would "crush the pride of Nimai Pandita", and that "the joy of Nityananda", who went freely about the town preaching the name, "would soon come to nothing" (23.110–113). The frightened devotees came to the Lord:

“‘We can no longer hold kirtana, for we fear the Kazi. With thousands of his followers he prowls everywhere. Soon we shall have to leave Navadvipa and go wherever our eyes lead us.’” (CB, Madhya 23.116–117)

"Today I Shall Hold Kirtana Throughout the Town"

According to the “Charitamrita”, the townspeople told the Lord everything, and He answered them as only He can who has come to give the world sankirtana:

“The Lord ordered, ‘Go and hold kirtana! Today I shall destroy all the Muslims.’” (CC, Adi 17.130)

Vrindavana Dasa tells that when the Lord heard of the obstacle to the kirtana, He blazed with anger like Rudra: "Today I shall hold kirtana throughout Navadvipa. Let Me see who will do anything to Me! Today let Me see — I shall burn the Kazi's house and door. Let Me see what his king will do! Today I shall pour down a vast rain of prema-bhakti" (CB, Madhya 23.118, 121–123). This anger is no worldly enmity, nor enmity towards Muslims: the Lord rises against the opposition to the sankirtana, and the fruit of His anger, as the story will show, is mercy to the Kazi. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that the teaching to be "humbler than grass" does not mean looking on indifferently while the service of Krishna is opposed; and the rain of prema-bhakti that the Lord promises is, for the unbelievers, the very death of their unbelief.6

The townspeople went home and went on singing, but fear of the Kazi did not leave their hearts. Seeing this, the Lord called them together:

“‘Today I shall hold kirtana throughout the town. By evening, all of you, decorate the town. In the evening light lamps in every house, and we shall see what Kazi comes to stop Me!’” (CC, Adi 17.133–134)

According to the “Chaitanya-bhagavata”, everyone who wished to see the power of Krishna was to take a great torch, and the Lord heartened them all: "Countless universes are the servants of My servants. What is there to fear, when I am with you?" (Madhya 23.125–127). The “Bhakti-ratnakara” recalls that every house held a festival, hundreds of thousands of lamps burned, and the night became like day (2.303–304).

The Night Procession

In the evening the Lord went out of His house and divided the kirtana into three parts. The “Charitamrita” names them:

“Haridasa danced in the first group, and in the middle one Acharya Gosani danced in great joy. In the last group danced Gaurachandra, and Nityananda Prabhu danced along with Him.” (CC, Adi 17.136–137)7

With the Lord went Gadadhara, Vakreshvara, Murari, Srivasa, Gopinatha and countless other servants of His; Vrindavana Dasa names many of the singers (CB, Madhya 23.150–152). The biographies, telling of other associates, remember that on that night the Lord was accompanied by Nityananda and all the Vaishnavas, by Srivasa, Vakreshvara, Advaita, who led one of the parts of the procession, Chandrashekhara, Gangadasa, Nandana Acharya, Murari, to whom one of the leading roles in the procession is given, Jagadisha, Govinda Ghosha, Vasudeva Datta, Haridasa at the head of one of the parts, and Gadadhara Pandita.8

Krishnadasa Kaviraja says that Vrindavana Dasa described these pastimes at length (Adi 17.138), and himself gives only the essentials:

“So, holding kirtana, He wandered through the town, and in His wandering He came to the Kazi's door. The people shouted threats and made a great uproar: under Gaurachandra's protection they had grown wild with boldness. At the sound of the kirtana the Kazi hid in his house, and hearing the threats and roars, he would not come out.” (CC, Adi 17.139–141)

Vrindavana Dasa traces the route of the procession from ghata to ghata along the Ganga: from the Lord's own ghata to Madhai's ghata, past Barakona-ghata and Nagariya-ghata, through Ganganagara to Simulia (CB, Madhya 23.299–300, 348); the “Anubhashya” lists them in the same way.

In Vrindavana Dasa the Kazi, hearing singing and music from afar, first wonders, "Is it a wedding, or a kirtana of ghosts?" and sends his servants to find out who has broken his ban. The servants come back in fear: millions of people with blazing torches are shouting "Death to the Kazi!", and at their head is Nimai, now weeping, now so fierce that He seems ready to swallow everyone. The Kazi thinks that Nimai Pandita is going to be married, and vows to strip of caste all who have broken his ban — but then the thunder of the kirtana breaks out, and he and his servants run about not knowing where to flee, "like a frog or a mouse trying in fear to escape a snake". Some of the servants threw off their turbans, mingled with the crowd and, unrecognised, trembling with fear, danced in the kirtana (CB, Madhya 23.359–386). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that at first the Kazi took the procession for a wedding or some festivity.

Then the crowd fell upon the Kazi's house:

“Unruly people broke into the Kazi's house and flower garden; Vrindavana dasa has described this at length.” (CC, Adi 17.142)

In Vrindavana Dasa the Lord in His anger demands that the Kazi be brought and orders his house to be broken and set on fire, and the people smash rooms and doors, break the mango and jackfruit trees and tear up the flower garden; the “Bhakti-ratnakara” too says that with the cry "Beat the Kazi!" the people broke his house, gate and flower garden (2.308–309). But here too the Lord's anger is only His play. The devotees, with cloth wrapped round their necks, fell at His feet and began to pray to Him, reminding Him that the Vedas call Him free from anger and ever blissful:

“‘You have punished the Kazi enough. If he obstructs the kirtana again, then You may kill him.’” (CB, Madhya 23.414)

“Hearing the prayers of His devotees, Mahaprabhu smiled. Then He left that place, chanting the name of Hari and delighting in the bliss of the dance.” (CB, Madhya 23.417)

And so Vrindavana Dasa's account of the Kazi ends: the procession moves on.9

A Guest at the Kazi's Door

What happened next Vrindavana Dasa did not describe, and the “Charitamrita” fills out his account (Adi 17.138, 142); so Srila Bhaktivinoda too explains in his introduction to the chapter. The wrecking of the house and the devotees' prayers we know from Vrindavana Dasa; the Lord's conversation with the Kazi, from Krishnadasa Kaviraja.

“Then Mahaprabhu sat down at his door and sent respectable men to call the Kazi. The Kazi approached from a distance, his head bowed, and the Lord received him with honour and gave him a seat.” (CC, Adi 17.143–144)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta notes that the Lord honoured the Kazi according to worldly custom. The Lord, who seeks no honour for Himself and honours everyone, approached the Kazi too not by force but by courtesy: He called him through respectable men.10

“The Lord said, ‘I have come to you as a guest, yet when you saw Me you hid. What kind of conduct is this?’ The Kazi said, ‘You came in anger, so I stayed hidden to let You grow calm. Now that You are calm, I have come to meet You. How fortunate I am to receive a guest like You!’” (CC, Adi 17.145–147)

And the Kazi reminded the Lord of the kinship that joined them through their village:

“‘By village kinship Chakravarti is my uncle, and village kinship is truer than kinship of the body. Nilambara Chakravarti is Your maternal grandfather, so by that relation You are my nephew. An uncle will bear his nephew's anger, and a nephew does not hold his uncle's offences against him.’” (CC, Adi 17.148–150)

In the Bengali the Kazi says that by village kinship (grama-sambandhe) Chakravarti is his chacha, his paternal uncle; the “Anubhashya” explains that Nilambara Chakravarti is meant. And Srila Bhaktivinoda explains where this kinship came from: the old house of the Kazi's family stands in one part of the village of Brahmana-pushkarini, and its other part adjoins Taranavasa, the former Bilva-pushkarini; this was one village, and so the Lord was the Kazi's "nephew". Later the Lord too will call him "uncle" (mama, Adi 17.172).11

“So the two spoke in hints, and no one could grasp the inner meaning.” (CC, Adi 17.151)

What these hints concealed Krishnadasa Kaviraja does not say, and we shall not interpret them ourselves.

“The Lord said, ‘I have come to ask you a question,’ and the Kazi replied, ‘Ask whatever is on Your mind.’” (CC, Adi 17.152)

The Cow and the Bull

The Lord's first question concerned the killing of cows:

“The Lord said, ‘You drink cow's milk, so the cow is your mother; the bull produces grain, so he is your father. You kill your father and mother and eat them — what religion is this? On what authority do you commit such a sin?’” (CC, Adi 17.153–154)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that the bull is the farmer's greatest helper: with him the land is ploughed, and man gets his grain.

The Kazi answered from his own scripture. As the Hindus have the Vedas and Puranas, he said, so the Muslims have the Koran; the Koran speaks of two paths, the path of worldly engagement (pravritti) and the path of renunciation (nivritti). For those on the path of renunciation the killing of living beings is forbidden, while on the path of worldly engagement there is an injunction to kill cows, and if it is done by the order of scripture there is no sin; and the Vedas too, he added, speak of the killing of cows, and great sages did it of old (CC, Adi 17.155–158). The “Anubhashya” notes that Islam distinguishes three paths: sharia, tariqa and marifa.

The Lord answered that the Vedas strictly forbid the killing of cows, and that the words about sacrifice mean something else:

“So the sages would kill a worn-out old animal (jaradgava) and restore its life by Vedic mantras. The old animal became young once more, so this was not killing but a kindness. In the age of Kali the brahmanas have no such power, and so now no one kills cows.” (CC, Adi 17.161–163)

The Lord quoted a verse of the “Brahma-vaivarta Purana”: five things are forbidden in the age of Kali — the horse sacrifice, the cow sacrifice, sannyasa, the offering of flesh to the forefathers, and the begetting of a son by the husband's brother (CC, Adi 17.164). And He concluded:

“‘You cannot bring them back to life; all you do is kill. For you there is no escape from hell. For as many thousands of years as there are hairs on a cow's body, the killer of a cow rots in the hell of Raurava. The one who gave you your scripture was himself mistaken; not knowing the essence of scripture, he gave such an order.’” (CC, Adi 17.165–167)

The Vedic sacrifice of an old cow (jaradgava) was not killing, because the mantras gave her back her life and youth; but in the age of Kali no one has such power, and so this sacrifice is forbidden. "Mistaken," Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains, means approving needless violence to living beings.12

“Hearing this, the Kazi was dumbstruck and could find no words. After some thought he admitted defeat and said: ‘What You have said, Pandita, is true. Our scriptures are recent and cannot stand up to reasoning. Our scripture is invented — I know that well; yet out of loyalty to my community I still accept it.’” (CC, Adi 17.168–170)

These are the Kazi's own words. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains their sense: "recent" means arisen in time, whereas the Veda is eternal and not made by man (apaurusheya); "invented" means born of the mind; and jati is the community the Kazi belonged to, and loyalty to it. Srila Bhaktivinoda in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” develops the same thought: all these books have a beginning, none is without beginning as the word of the Vedas is, and so arguments that lack a firm root are open to doubt; there too he names three scriptures of the yavanas — the ancient book of the Jews, the Koran and the Bible. One of the biographies puts this explanation into the Kazi's own mouth.13 The Lord had not come to the Kazi to win a debate: He was leading him to the holy name.

Why the Kazi Does Not Forbid the Kirtana

“The reasoning of the yavanas' scriptures is by nature unsound. Smiling, Mahaprabhu questioned him once more: ‘Let Me ask you one more question, uncle. Answer truly, and do not deceive Me with tricks. In your town there is sankirtana all the time — the din of drums and songs, singing and dancing. You are the Kazi, with authority to oppose the Hindu religion; I cannot understand why you do not forbid it now.’” (CC, Adi 17.171–174)

The Kazi answered, "Everyone calls You Gaurahari, and by that name I too shall address You. Listen, Gaurahari: if we can speak in private, I shall tell You the reason." The Lord said, "These people are My intimates. Speak plainly and have no fear" (CC, Adi 17.175–177).

And the Kazi told his dream. On the night when he had entered a Hindu's house, broken the mridanga and forbidden the sankirtana, there came to him a most terrible lion, with the body of a man and the face of a lion, roaring mightily. He leapt upon the sleeping Kazi:

“Pressing his claws into my chest, he said in a dreadful voice, ‘I will tear your chest open in return for the mridanga! You forbid My kirtana — I will destroy you!’ Terrified, I shut my eyes and trembled. Seeing my fear, the lion grew kind and said, ‘I have humbled you only to teach you a lesson. That day you did no great harm, so I have forgiven you and spared your life. But if you do such a thing again, I will not bear it: I will destroy you with your whole family, and the yavanas too.’ With these words the lion went away, but I was filled with fear. Look — here are the marks of his claws on my chest!” (CC, Adi 17.181–186)

The man's body with a lion's face, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains, is Sri Nrisimhadeva, who destroys enmity towards the devotees, towards bhakti and towards the Lord. His anger was mercy: He humbled the Kazi in order to teach him. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says that on the eve of the procession the Lord Himself became Nrisimha to tear open the Kazi's chest; the Kazi saw it with his own eyes, understood that Nimai was no mere man, and told everyone of it (2.310–311). In Govinda-deva too the Lord first terrified the Kazi in the form of Nrisimha and only then set out with the procession (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 5.42).14

“So saying, the Kazi bared his chest, and all who heard and saw were amazed.” (CC, Adi 17.187)

The Kazi confessed that until then he had told no one of it.

That same day, he went on, one of his men had come to him (a piyada, which, the “Anubhashya” explains, means a servant of the lowest rank, a messenger): "I went to stop the kirtana, and suddenly a tongue of fire struck my face. My whole beard was burnt and my face was blistered." Every one of the men whom the Kazi sent to forbid the kirtana told the same story (CC, Adi 17.188–190).

“Seeing all this, I was seized with great fear; now I stay at home and do not forbid the kirtana.” (CC, Adi 17.191)

So the Kazi let the townspeople sing the kirtana freely.

The Complaints of the Muslims and the Unbelievers

Then the Muslims came to the Kazi with a complaint: the Hindu religion had grown beyond all bounds in the town, nothing could be heard but "Hari! Hari!", the Hindus cried "Krishna! Krishna!", laughed and wept, danced and rolled in the dust; "If the Padshah hears of it, you will pay for it" (CC, Adi 17.192–195). The “Anubhashya” gives the definition of a mleccha: one who eats beef, says much that is contrary to the Vedas and is devoid of all good conduct. Srila Bhaktivinoda and one of the biographies give the complainants' words more fully: though the Padshah is your kinsman, he can still punish you.

The Kazi asked them: it is natural for Hindus to say "Hari", but why do you, Muslims, keep taking the names of the Hindus' God? And one of them answered:

“One of them said, ‘I used to make fun of the Hindus. Some of them are called Krishnadasa, some Ramadasa, some Haridasa, and they were forever saying "Hari! Hari!" — I thought they meant to steal someone's wealth. Ever since then my tongue keeps saying "Hari! Hari!" I do not want it to, yet it says it — what can I do?’” (CC, Adi 17.198–200)

Srila Bhaktivinoda explains his jest: in Bengali hari can also mean "I steal", and so the Muslim decided that those who kept saying "Hari" were planning to steal someone's goods. Another Muslim confessed that his tongue too, after he had mocked the Hindus, kept repeating the name of Krishna without stopping, and he could not understand what spells and herbs the Hindus knew (CC, Adi 17.201–202). Yet this is not sorcery but the power of the name itself. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that mockery is one of the four kinds of namabhasa, the shadow of the holy name: "The name of Vaikuntha, uttered to indicate something else, in jest, to fill out a song, or with contempt, destroys all sins" (SB 6.2.14).15

When he had heard them, the Kazi sent the Muslims home. Then five or seven Hindu unbelievers came to complain of Nimai: since His return from Gaya He was undermining the foundations of dharma, singing loudly and clapping His hands, so that no one could sleep for the mridangas and karatalas; He chanted the name of Krishna with the low-born, and the great mantra of the holy name, heard by everyone, was losing its power; "You are the lord of this place, and all its people are yours. Summon Nimai and drive Him out" (CC, Adi 17.203–213). The Kazi soothed them and promised to stop Nimai's sankirtana (17.214). These unbelievers (pashandis), Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains, are people sunk in ritual, worshippers of many gods, hostile to Vishnu and the Vaishnavas.

"You Are Narayana"

Having told all this, the Kazi concluded:

“‘The great God of the Hindus is Narayana — and my heart tells me that You are He.’” (CC, Adi 17.215)

“Hearing this, Mahaprabhu smiled and, touching the Kazi, began to speak: ‘Krishna's name in your mouth — this is most wonderful! Your sins are destroyed, and you have become supremely pure. You have spoken three names — Hari, Krishna and Narayana. You are most fortunate and most pious.’” (CC, Adi 17.216–218)

Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that namabhasa, the shadow of the holy name that destroys sins, had arisen in the Kazi's mouth. So the Lord's mercy, which began with the terror of Nrisimha, brought the Kazi to the name.16

“At these words tears fell from the Kazi's eyes, and touching the Lord's feet, he said with deep feeling: ‘By Your grace my evil mind is gone. Be merciful to me, so that devotion to You may abide in me.’” (CC, Adi 17.219–220)

The Lord asked the Kazi for only one thing: let there be no more obstruction to the sankirtana anywhere in Nadia.

“The Kazi said, ‘On all who are born in my line I shall lay a solemn charge (talak): they shall never obstruct the kirtana.’” (CC, Adi 17.222)

Srila Bhaktivinoda explains that talak is a solemn oath. The biographies record the same vow: neither the Kazi nor anyone of his family or his people would hinder the sankirtana of the Vaishnavas, whether in houses or in the streets; one of them says that the Kazi became a friend of the Vaishnavas.

“Thereupon the Lord rose, crying ‘Hari!’, and all the Vaishnavas rose with Him, raising the sound of Hari's name. The Lord set off to go on with the kirtana, and the Kazi walked along with Him, his heart full of joy. Then the son of Shachi bade the Kazi farewell and came back to His own home, dancing all the way.” (CC, Adi 17.223–225)

Srila Bhaktivinoda in the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya” adds that on that night of the first town kirtana Chand Kazi went with the kirtana right up to Shridhara's courtyard and turned back from there. And the Lord, on His way home, entered Shridhara's poor dwelling and drank water from his old iron pot (CC, Adi 17.70; CB, Madhya 23.428–437); according to the “Chaitanya-bhagavata”, He had first passed, dancing, through the villages of the conch-shell merchants and the weavers.

So Krishnadasa Kaviraja ends this account:

“Thus the Lord showed His grace to the Kazi. Whoever hears of it is freed from his offences.” (CC, Adi 17.226)

The biographies retell the whole conversation after the “Charitamrita” and Srila Bhaktivinoda's commentary, sometimes more briefly and in their own words.

Descendants and Places of Remembrance

The Kazi kept his word. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Anubhashya” that his descendants live in the same place to this day and join in the sankirtana of Krishna's name, raising no objection to it at all.

The tomb (samadhi) of Chand Kazi still stands in Bamunpukur, in Sri Mayapura; the “Anubhashya” also says that it has been preserved. One of the biographies adds that a very old golok-champa tree grows beside it and that the tomb is honoured by Hindus and Muslims alike. To the same neighbourhood belong the lane of Vamana-pukura, where, according to the “Gaudiya-bhashya”, the Kazi's house stood, and the village of Brahmana-pushkarini, where, according to the “Amrita-pravaha-bhashya”, the old house of his family stands. One of the biographies lists "Chand Kazi's Samadhi, Sridham Mayapur" among the maths and preaching centres founded by Srila Prabhupada Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati. When and how the Kazi left this world the sources do not say.

In Sri Mayapura there is also the well-known spot Khola-bhangar-danga, "the place where the mridanga was broken" (so too in the “Anubhashya”). According to one of the biographies, Srila Jagannatha Dasa Babaji by his divine vision pointed out first the place of the Lord's appearance and then this spot too, and it is Srivasa's courtyard, Srivasa-angana, where Mahaprabhu sang His night kirtanas.17

Not far from the Kazi's tomb stands Shridhara's house too, to whose courtyard the Kazi came with the kirtana.18

The Lord's Mercy

The Kazi who had opposed the kirtana received the Lord's mercy. That is why one of the biographies calls him "the devotee", and another says that he became a devotee of Mahaprabhu. Gaurasundara Himself, in Sridham Mayapura, the place of His appearance, came at the head of the sankirtana to his house and made him utter the name of Hari. The “Bhakti-ratnakara” says that Gaurasundara, the Purifier of the fallen, showed mercy to the fortunate Kazi, and hearing of it, noble people knew for certain that Gaurachandra is Narayana (2.317–318). Govinda-deva writes that the Lord, who loves even mlecchas, cast aside his scripture and instructed him in the true scripture (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 5.44), and the “Advaita-prakasha” that the deliverance of Jagai and Madhai and the deliverance of the Kazi amazed the people (14.156); Murari Gupta says only in general terms that the Lord delivered mlecchas and others (2.17.11). The sources tell nothing more of him; but by the Lord's mercy he uttered the holy name, prayed with tears for devotion and vowed for all his line never to hinder the sankirtana.

In this story we see how Mahaprabhu removes the obstacles to sankirtana. His anger protects the kirtana but does not destroy the opponent: Nrisimha terrifies the Kazi in order to teach him; the Lord comes to him as a guest and a "nephew", questions him courteously and leads him to the holy name — and he who had forbidden the kirtana himself walks after it. And as the instruments of worldly pujas came to serve the Hari-kirtana, so the ruler who had opposed the name vowed never to hinder it again.

The Lord's servants followed in His footsteps. So Gadadhara Dasa made the fearsome kazi of his own village, Ariadaha, utter the name of Hari: the servant walks the path of his Master.19

Notes

  1. One of the biographies gives only the first name: "Sirajuddin Chand Kazi".
  2. The sources differ as to where the Kazi broke the mridanga. According to the “Chaitanya-bhagavata”, he was passing along the road; according to the “Charitamrita” (Adi 17.125), he came "to one house". One of the biographies writes that he came to Srivasa's house, broke a mridanga there and had some of the devotees beaten to frighten the rest; another, that the Kazi, hearing the talk of Nityananda's preaching and the noise of the kirtana, broke the mridanga of the sankirtana. We follow the original sources.
  3. According to the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (12.3089), it was the unbelievers who informed the Kazi; according to the “Gaura-krishnodaya” (5.40–41), the heretics, after which the yavana ruler sent his men, and they, with oaths and spies, forbade the kirtana in every house.
  4. Of the opponents of the kirtana Srila Bhaktisiddhanta writes in the “Gaudiya-bhashya” that, being in power, they oppressed the townspeople in the name of religion; one of the biographies applies these words to the Kazi himself. We give no worldly, political judgement of the ruler or of his times: the Kazi opposed the kirtana, and the Lord subdued him and showed him mercy.
  5. The unbelievers (pashandis) here are not the Hindus in general. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta calls them "so-called Hindus", and in the “Anubhashya” people sunk in ritual, worshippers of many gods, hostile to Vishnu and the Vaishnavas.
  6. The words "Today I shall destroy all the Muslims" (literally, "all the yavanas", CC, Adi 17.130) and "I shall burn the Kazi's house" (CB, Madhya 23.122, 388–405) are the play of the Lord protecting the sankirtana, not worldly enmity towards Muslims. In the same chapter of the “Charitamrita” Muslims repeat the Lord's names in spite of themselves (17.198–202), and Haridasa Thakura, born in a Muslim family, is one of Mahaprabhu's closest associates. The devotees remind the Lord that He is free from anger (CB, Madhya 23.406–414), and He smiles and goes on with the kirtana; and the outcome of His anger is mercy to the Kazi (CC, Adi 17.226).
  7. The “Chaitanya-bhagavata” gives the order differently: Advaita in front, Haridasa in the middle, Srivasa at the rear (Madhya 23.141–143). In the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (12.3092–3095) there are the companies of Advaita, Haridasa, Srivasa, the Lord with Nityananda and Gadadhara, and Vakreshvara; in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” (5.43) Advaita goes in front, Nityananda the avadhuta behind, and Haridasa dances in the middle. One of the biographies says that the Lord took the procession along the Ganga's bank and danced in front of it Himself; but according to the “Charitamrita” He was in the last group, and according to the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” (Madhya 23.425) the devotees danced in front and He followed. We follow the “Charitamrita”.
  8. One of the biographies, writing of Jagadisha, refers here to "“Chaitanya-bhagavata”, Madhya 13.150"; the correct reference is Madhya 23.150.
  9. In the “Chaitanya-bhagavata” the Kazi does not come out to the Lord, and there is no conversation; it is given by the “Charitamrita”. We bring the two accounts together without mixing them: the wrecking of the house and the devotees' prayers after Vrindavana Dasa, the conversation after Krishnadasa Kaviraja.
  10. One of the biographies adds that the Lord asked respectable neighbours to tell the Kazi that He had come without ill will, and the Kazi, touched by His courtesy, came out. According to the “Bhakti-ratnakara” (2.315–316), the Kazi himself, in great fear and with tears, went to the Lord and surrendered to Him; according to the “Gaura-krishnodaya” (5.44), he came out to Him at once in fear and took shelter of Him with all his heart. We follow the “Charitamrita”.
  11. One of the biographies calls the Kazi, by village kinship, Nilambara Chakravarti's "brother". This is a mistake: according to the “Charitamrita” (Adi 17.148–149) Nilambara is his "uncle", and so the Lord, Nilambara's grandson, is his "nephew".
  12. The verse on the five things forbidden in Kali is from the “Brahma-vaivarta Purana”, Krishna-janma-khanda 185.180; it is also quoted in the “Malamasa-tattva”. The Lord's words do not approve of animal sacrifice: the ancient sacrifice was a kindness to the old cow only because the mantras restored her life, and now that no one has such power, it is forbidden.
  13. There is no list of three scriptures in the verses of the “Charitamrita”: it is Srila Bhaktivinoda's commentary. We give the Kazi's words about his scriptures as they stand in the “Charitamrita”, without polemic and without disrespect for anyone's faith.
  14. There is no contradiction here: according to the “Charitamrita”, the dream came on the night the Kazi broke the mridanga, that is, before the procession; the “Bhakti-ratnakara” says "on the eve", and the “Gaura-krishnodaya” that the Lord terrified the Kazi with Nrisimha and then set out with the procession. One of the biographies adds that Nrisimha forgave the Kazi on condition that he would not hinder the kirtana.
  15. The Muslim's words about "spells and herbs" are only his own bewilderment.
  16. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta calls what the Kazi uttered namabhasa: it destroys sins, but it is not yet the pure name, whose fruit is prema. So we do not exaggerate his position; yet neither do we belittle it: the Lord calls him fortunate, and the Kazi himself prays with tears for devotion.
  17. The “Anubhashya” calls Khola-bhangar-danga simply "a spot in Mayapura"; the identification with Srivasa-angana is made by one of the biographies. According to the “Chaitanya-bhagavata”, the Kazi broke the mridanga on the road; according to the “Charitamrita”, "in one house" (see note 2).
  18. According to one of the biographies, Shridhara's house stands a mile to the east of Chand Kazi's tomb, at the edge of Mayapura near Saradanga; according to another, on the northern edge of Mayapura, to the south-east of Chand Kazi's samadhi; today it is Shridhara-angana.
  19. This is a different kazi, the ruler of Ariadaha (CC, Adi 10.53; CB, Antya 5). Chand Kazi should also not be confused with the kazi who persecuted Haridasa Thakura (CB, Adi 16), with Malaya Kazi of the “Prema-vilasa”, or with Khanaulla Kazi, Haridasa's father according to the “Advaita-vilasa”.
